analysis.one_liner: Requires cash compensation for flight delays and bumping, bans seat shrinking, and curbs airline junk fees.
analysis.headline: The Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights, with 9 Senate supporters, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2023 and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give airline passengers a set of enforceable rights: at least $1,350 in cash if you are bumped from an oversold flight, automatic refunds plus meal and hotel coverage when a flight the airline controls is delayed or cancelled, a ban on shrinking seats and legroom while minimum seat standards are written, and rules forcing airlines to charge only fees that are reasonable and proportional to their costs. It would also let passengers sue airlines directly, void the forced-arbitration and class-action-waiver clauses in airline tickets and loyalty programs, raise penalties for violating passenger rules, and require a study of how airline mergers since 2000 affected fares and choice.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers — especially those bumped from oversold flights or stranded by controllable delays and cancellations, families charged extra to sit with their children, and travelers hit with baggage, change, and seat-selection fees. People with disabilities gain lavatory accommodations and a new right to sue over discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers, especially delayed and bumped flyers

how_it_helps.text: Passengers involuntarily denied boarding on an oversold flight must be paid at least $1,350 in cash, removing the current dollar caps on bumping compensation. [S3]

If a flight the airline controls (crew scheduling, maintenance, IT, baggage handling) is delayed or cancelled, the airline must automatically refund the ticket, rebook the passenger at no extra cost, and pay $1,350 cash plus a meal for delays over 4 hours, and cover a hotel if the departure slips to the next day. [S3]
The FAA must immediately bar airlines from shrinking seat width, pitch, legroom, or aisle width, and then write minimum seat-size standards for passenger safety and health. [S3]

Airlines may only charge fees for bag handling, seat selection, and flight changes or cancellations that are reasonable and proportional to their actual costs, and children 13 and under must be seated with their accompanying adult at no extra charge. [S3]

Passengers get a private right of action to sue airlines over unfair and deceptive practices and discrimination, and pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in airline tickets, loyalty programs, and airline credit products are voided — so disputes go to court, not a company-chosen arbitrator. [S3]

Civil penalties for violating passenger protection laws are increased, airlines are barred from negotiating those penalties down, and airlines must notify passengers of their rights and refund eligibility within 30 minutes of becoming aware of it. [S3]
Airlines must provide functional, disability-accessible lavatories and free potable water on board, and must train front-line employees on passenger rights every 180 days. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Major airlines and their loyalty-program partners, who would pay cash compensation for delays and bumping, lose fee revenue that regulators judge disproportionate to their costs, face higher civil penalties they can no longer negotiate down, and lose forced arbitration and class-action waivers in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major airlines and loyalty-program credit partners

drawbacks.text: The $1,350 cash compensation applies to delays of more than 4 hours caused by anything within the airline's control — a category that includes crew scheduling and IT systems — which could push airlines to cancel marginal flights earlier rather than risk running them late, and the added cost would likely flow into ticket prices. [S3]

Requiring fees to be proportional to actual costs, covering hotels for overnight delays, and enforcing seat-size minimums would raise airline operating costs, some portion of which is likely to appear in fares. [S3]

The bill's ban on pre-dispute arbitration applies not just to tickets but to airline reward programs and credit products, a broad reach that goes well beyond the delay-and-fee problems the bill is mainly aimed at, and the new private rights of action could generate substantial litigation. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers, the protections are concrete and enforceable — cash when you are bumped or stranded, automatic refunds, a seat next to your child at no charge, seats that cannot legally keep shrinking. The costs are real but ordinary for consumer regulation: some pass-through to fares and a possible incentive to cancel flights early rather than run them late. The litigation and arbitration provisions are broader than they needed to be. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose benefits to travelers outweigh its costs, and it never got a serious look.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2023, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights on January 31, 2023, joined by Senators Markey, Whitehouse, Casey, Wyden, and Sanders as original cosponsors. [S1][S5]
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. [S5]
That referral was the bill's last action of record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action appears in its action history through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S5][S1]
The bill ended the Congress with 9 total Senate supporters — Senator Blumenthal plus 8 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on. [S4]

Had it passed, it would have required the Transportation Department to write rules on bumping compensation, delay and cancellation refunds, seat-size minimums, and fee proportionality within roughly 180 days of enactment. [S2][S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major airlines and their loyalty-program credit partners are better off: the compensation mandates, fee restrictions, seat-size freeze, and loss of forced arbitration never took effect, and the fee and loyalty revenue the bill would have constrained continued untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines and loyalty credit partners

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 31, 2023 and recruited five colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, Sen. Bob Casey, Sen. Ron Wyden, and Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 9 senators.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 31, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining two years of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for committee consideration at any point in the 118th Congress.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of them cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no bipartisan base that might have pushed committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; 0 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill targets the airline industry's core revenue practices: involuntary-bumping compensation would rise to a $1,350 cash floor, controllable delays would trigger automatic refunds plus $1,350, meals, and hotels, ancillary fees would have to be proportional to actual costs, and seat dimensions could not shrink further. Airlines' interest in keeping these revenue streams runs directly against the passenger protections ordinary travelers would have gained. [S3]

industries.industry: Airline loyalty programs and co-brand credit card issuers
industries.note: The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers in reward-program and airline credit-product contracts, and requires standardized disclosure of how miles are earned and redeemed, including successful-redemption rates. Loyalty programs are a major profit center for airlines and their bank partners, and those partners' interest in keeping disputes out of court ran against passengers' ability to sue. [S3]

industries.industry: Online travel agents, metasearch engines, and ticket agents
industries.note: The bill requires airlines to hand over complete, usable fare, fee, and tax data to online travel agents and metasearch engines and lets customers complete full purchases through them, ending airline practices of withholding information from third-party search tools. [S3]
